evidence.title: Evidence depends on the treatment setting
evidence.intro: Adjuvant and advanced trials answer different questions.
evidence.population: Resected Ex19del/L858R disease; untreated advanced Ex19del/L858R disease; or advanced T790M disease after an earlier EGFR inhibitor.
evidence.interpretation: The evidence differs by setting. In a study after complete surgery, adjuvant osimertinib improved survival compared with placebo. In untreated advanced EGFR-mutated cancer, it improved survival compared with older EGFR tablets. After resistance with T790M, it delayed progression compared with platinum/pemetrexed, but the final overall-survival comparison was not statistically significant. These results describe selected study groups and cannot predict your own outcome.
evidence.limitations: Study averages cannot give an individual prognosis or compare today’s treatment options head to head. Chemotherapy-combination and post-chemoradiation studies require a separate discussion.

support.title: Nausea medicines
support.text: Osimertinib has minimal-to-low oral emetic risk. Routine infusion premedication is not usually needed. Agree rescue medicines individually, including QT and interaction review; do not copy a chemotherapy antiemetic course.

support.title: Medicine interactions
support.text: Tell the team about all medicines and supplements. Do not take St John’s wort. Strong enzyme-inducing medicines and medicines that affect heart rhythm require pharmacy review before changes.

ADAURA randomised completely resected stage IB–IIIA Ex19del/L858R disease, with or without prior adjuvant chemotherapy; survival runs from randomisation, not surgery or diagnosis. Stage II–IIIA and overall IB–IIIA results are separate.

FLAURA enrolled untreated advanced Ex19del/L858R NSCLC and compared older EGFR TKIs; it does not establish outcomes for every uncommon activating mutation or superiority over contemporary combination options.

Previous ILD, drug-induced ILD, steroid-treated radiation pneumonitis or active ILD were clinical-study exclusions; assess before treatment.
Baseline QTc >470 ms was a trial exclusion; congenital long QT is a separate NCCP exclusion.

NCCP advises closer monitoring for age >65 years or body weight <50 kg; EMA does not require dose adjustment solely for age or weight.

questions.q: Does taking capsules mean fewer important risks?
questions.a: Capsules are cancer treatment and can cause serious side effects. Keep the planned tests and use the oncology contact plan for new symptoms.

questions.q: Does having side effects show it is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably indicate cancer response; your team assesses benefit using the relevant follow-up plan.

questions.q: How long will I take alectinib?
questions.a: Take alectinib twice daily with food, every day, with no planned rest week. After surgery, treatment lasts up to 24 months, stopping sooner for recurrence or unacceptable side effects. For advanced cancer, treatment continues until progression or unacceptable side effects under the oncology plan.

questions.q: What if I miss a dose or vomit?
questions.a: If a dose is missed, take it only if the next dose is more than 6 hours away. If the next dose is due within 6 hours, skip the missed dose. Do not take two doses together. If you vomit after a dose, take the next dose at its usual time; do not take an extra dose.

questions.q: Which blood tests happen early?
questions.a: Liver tests are planned every 2 weeks for 3 months. CPK is checked every 2 weeks for the first month. Blood count and kidney tests are checked every 4 weeks; symptoms may prompt extra tests.

questions.q: When is my next ECG?
questions.a: NCCP asks for an ECG before its second treatment cycle, but this medicine is taken continuously. Ask the team to confirm the first repeat ECG appointment and later checks.

questions.q: Can I change or restart my dose myself?
questions.a: No. If alectinib is held or reduced, ask what needs to recover, when review happens and who will authorise restarting.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the medicine name, current dose, last dose, symptoms and when they began. Explain whether you can drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide whether tests are safe?
questions.a: No. Blood results, symptoms, current dose and treatment history need the prescriber’s assessment. This guide does not authorise treatment.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates?
questions.a: No. This map shows general timing. Your hospital arranges actual appointments.

support_plans.label: Alectinib daily oral treatment
additional_support: Alectinib is minimal-to-low oral emetic risk. Treat nausea with prescribed as-required medicine if needed. Routine preventive anti-sickness treatment and infusion premedication are not required; your team selects a suitable rescue medicine.

The usual starting dose is 600 mg twice daily: four 150 mg capsules each time, taken with food. Use your own prescription, which may specify a lower dose. Swallow capsules whole; do not open or dissolve them. If a dose is missed, take it only if the next dose is more than 6 hours away. If the next dose is due within 6 hours, skip the missed dose. Do not take two doses together. If you vomit after a dose, take the next dose at its usual time; do not take an extra dose.
Keep liver, CPK and blood-count appointments. Muscle symptoms, jaundice, dark urine, unusual fatigue, cough or breathlessness need prompt review even between appointments.

Tell the team about dizziness, fainting and medicines that slow the pulse. Check new prescriptions, supplements, grapefruit and Seville oranges with pharmacy; interactions may require closer monitoring rather than an automatic dose change.
Avoid prolonged sunlight during treatment and for at least 7 days after stopping. Use broad-spectrum UVA/UVB sunscreen and lip balm SPF 50 or higher.

Women who could become pregnant need highly effective contraception during treatment and for at least 5 weeks afterwards. Men with female partners who could become pregnant need highly effective contraception during treatment and for at least 3 months afterwards. Oral contraceptive effectiveness may be reduced: ask for a suitable method. Do not breastfeed during treatment. Discuss fertility before treatment and contact the team promptly if pregnancy occurs.

items.title: Baseline and ongoing checks

items.title: Interaction review
items.text: Some antibiotics, antifungals, antivirals, seizure medicines and herbal products can alter treatment. Your oncology pharmacist must review the complete medicine list. Do not change existing medicines yourself.

items.title: Sun protection
items.text: Avoid prolonged sun exposure during treatment and for at least five days afterwards. Use protective clothing, a hat, broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher sunscreen and lip balm. Report severe rash or sun reaction.

items.title: Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility
items.text: Discuss fertility before treatment. Tell the team promptly about possible pregnancy. Breastfeeding must stop during treatment.

questions.q: Why does the dose start lower?
questions.a: The initial seven-day lead-in is part of the brigatinib schedule and helps reduce early pulmonary reactions. Only increase when the team confirms it is appropriate.

questions.q: What if I miss or vomit a dose?
questions.a: Do not take an extra dose. Take the next scheduled dose at the usual time. Contact the team for ongoing vomiting or inability to keep fluids or medicine down.

questions.a: Do not restart or increase brigatinib yourself. A break because of a side effect follows a different recovery plan. Early lung inflammation can prevent the usual increase to 180 mg.

questions.q: Does the first-week breathing warning stop after day seven?
questions.a: No. Early reactions are especially important, but lung inflammation can also happen later. Report new or worsening breathing symptoms immediately.

questions.q: How long will I take brigatinib?
questions.a: There is no fixed number of cycles. Your team reviews benefit, side effects, scans and your priorities and agrees whether to continue, change or stop.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide whether tests are safe for treatment?
questions.a: No. The clinical team combines the protocol, symptoms, previous dose changes and organ function before prescribing.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent discussion?
questions.a: Your treatment aim, expected benefit and uncertainty, other options including not proceeding, serious and common harms, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for more time or explanation and reconsider the decision.

questions.q: Why is an ALK test needed?
questions.a: Lorlatinib is intended for cancers with a specific ALK change. Your team checks the result and whether the treatment fits your previous medicines.

questions.q: How long will I take it?
questions.a: Lorlatinib is taken once daily continuously, with no planned rest week. Treatment continues while it is helping and side effects remain acceptable; there is no fixed number of treatment cycles.

questions.q: What if I miss a dose or vomit?
questions.a: If a dose is missed, take it when remembered if the next dose is at least four hours away; otherwise skip it. Do not take two doses together. If you vomit after a dose, do not take another tablet; take the next dose at the usual time. These instructions follow the current product leaflet.

questions.q: Why are cholesterol tests needed if I feel well?
questions.a: Blood fats can rise without symptoms. Regular tests let the team treat this early. Raised cholesterol does not always mean lorlatinib must stop; your clinician uses the actual results and your overall condition.

questions.q: What changes should my family or friends notice?
questions.a: Changes in memory, concentration, mood, speech, behaviour or perceptions should be reported promptly. Agree with the team and someone you trust how changes will be noticed, if helpful.

questions.q: Can I drive?
questions.a: Lorlatinib can affect thinking and other CNS functions. Use caution and discuss driving or operating machinery, particularly if symptoms occur.

questions.q: Does a dose reduction mean treatment has failed?
questions.a: No. A hold or reduction may allow side effects to recover and reduce harm. The team reviews cancer control separately and explains the restart plan.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent discussion?
questions.a: Discuss your aim, expected benefits and uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, serious and lasting risks, daily practicalities, contraception, fertility, support needs and your right to reconsider.

questions.q: How long will I take treatment?
questions.a: The usual adult starting dose is 250 mg twice daily, every day, with no planned rest week. Use the strength and frequency on your own prescription. Treatment continues while it helps and side effects remain acceptable; there is no fixed course length.

questions.q: What if I miss a dose or vomit?
questions.a: Swallow 200 mg/250 mg hard capsules whole with water, with or without food; do not crush, dissolve or open them. Other formulations have different instructions. If a dose is missed, take it when remembered only if the next dose is at least 6 hours away; otherwise skip it. Never double a dose. If you vomit after a dose, do not take an extra dose; take the next dose at its usual time.

questions.q: Which checks happen most often at the start?
questions.a: Before starting: confirm the tumour test, blood count, kidney/liver tests, chest imaging, symptoms and all medicines; ECG and electrolytes near the first dose. Liver tests are planned weekly for the first 2 months using current product information, then monthly; NCCP says every 2 weeks initially, so confirm the local plan. Blood count and kidney tests are monthly. ECG, electrolytes, pulse and blood pressure need a planned schedule and earlier review if unwell. NCCP lists monthly chest X-ray; other disease imaging follows your consultant plan.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates?
questions.a: No. This map gives general milestones. Your team books actual appointments and authorises treatment changes.

questions.q: Why does my nausea plan need checking?
questions.a: Crizotinib has moderate-to-high oral sickness risk. Agree daily prevention and rescue treatment with your team. The chosen medicine must account for heart-rhythm and drug-interaction risks; do not add anti-sickness medicines or a prolonged steroid course yourself.

questions.q: Do side effects mean it is working?
questions.a: Side effects do not show whether cancer is responding. The team uses symptoms, examinations, imaging and other planned tests to assess benefit.

questions.q: What can studies tell me?
questions.a: In separate ALK studies, crizotinib delayed progression compared with the chemotherapy used at that time. The ROS1 study showed cancer responses but had no comparison group. These studies involve different populations and cannot rank present-day medicines or predict an individual outcome. Ask how the evidence fits your tumour, previous therapy, brain involvement and current alternatives.

items.title: Food and medicine interactions
items.text: Avoid grapefruit/grapefruit juice and St John’s wort. Check prescription medicines, pharmacy medicines, vitamins and herbal products before taking them. Some antibiotics, antifungals, heart medicines and seizure treatments interact. Do not stop a prescribed medicine without a plan.

items.title: Vision, driving and sunlight
items.text: Report visual changes. Take care with driving or machinery if vision, dizziness or fatigue affects safety. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and use protective clothing and sunscreen.

clinical.component_rationale: An ALK or ROS1 rearrangement can drive cancer growth. Crizotinib blocks these signals in suitable cancers. It can also affect healthy tissues, so regular tests and symptom reporting remain important.
key_points: Adult continuous oral crizotinib 250 mg twice daily; source reductions 200 mg twice daily then 250 mg once daily.
ALK previously treated 00243a; ROS1 00243b; ALK first-line 00243c. Confirm validated testing and local access.
Any suspected ILD: withhold; confirmed treatment-related any-grade ILD: permanently stop.
Grade-based hepatic, marrow, QT and bradycardia pathways require context and recurrence/dose history.
Moderate-high oral emetic risk; prophylaxis requires cardiac and interaction review.
NCCP p2: liver tests every 2 weeks for first 2 months; EMA SmPC 4.4 p11: weekly for first 2 months. Use weekly monitoring pending local reconciliation, then monthly; this supplement is explicit.
NCCP p3 renal table leaves CrCl exactly 30 mL/min unallocated (>30/<30). EMA p9 includes 30 in moderate impairment without starting reduction. Exact 30 and legacy ≤30 band require review.
NCCP p3 expects a 50% original dose in haemodialysis; EMA p9 severe-renal recommendation applies only without haemodialysis/peritoneal dialysis. Dialysis requires specialist individualisation.

NCCP p3 severe hepatic row contains QC alongside explicit 250 mg QD and permits increase if tolerated. EMA p9 specifies 250 mg once daily without a hepatic escalation schedule; do not automate escalation.
NCCP p3 grade 3 QT restart says 200 mg twice daily; EMA adult Table 4 says next lower dose. Existing dose and recurrence must be reconciled before restart.

NCCP p2 ECG every 2 cycles is not a defined time interval in this continuous oral regimen. Do not turn this into a fabricated 21/28-day cycle; arrange an explicit local ECG cadence with periodic ECG/electrolytes per SmPC.

support_summary: Crizotinib has moderate-to-high oral sickness risk. Agree daily prevention and rescue treatment with your team. The chosen medicine must account for heart-rhythm and drug-interaction risks; do not add anti-sickness medicines or a prolonged steroid course yourself.

Swallow 200 mg/250 mg hard capsules whole with water, with or without food; do not crush, dissolve or open them. Other formulations have different instructions. If a dose is missed, take it when remembered only if the next dose is at least 6 hours away; otherwise skip it. Never double a dose. rationale.summary: Crizotinib targets abnormal ALK or ROS1 signalling in selected advanced non-small-cell lung cancers. The aim is to control cancer and delay progression; the choice depends on the tumour test, previous treatment, other options and your priorities.

evidence.population: Separate adult advanced-NSCLC populations; preserve each study’s biomarker, treatment line and comparator.
evidence.comparison: Historical chemotherapy in ALK randomised trials; single-arm crizotinib in ROS1 cohort.
evidence.applicability: In separate ALK studies, crizotinib delayed progression compared with the chemotherapy used at that time. The ROS1 study showed cancer responses but had no comparison group. These studies involve different populations and cannot rank present-day medicines or predict an individual outcome. Ask how the evidence fits your tumour, previous therapy, brain involvement and current alternatives.

agents.name: Trifluridine/tipiracil
agents.mechanism: Damages cancer-cell DNA while slowing breakdown of the active drug
agents.explanation: Trifluridine is incorporated into DNA and interferes with cell growth. Tipiracil slows its breakdown so more trifluridine can reach the bloodstream. Healthy cells can also be affected; blood counts and symptoms need monitoring.

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

questions.q: What if I miss a dose or vomit?
questions.a: Do not make up a missed, held or vomited dose and do not double the next dose. Tell your team and follow the next scheduled dose on the agreed calendar. Repeated vomiting needs advice because of dehydration and missed medicines.

questions.q: Are tablet-free days safe days?
questions.a: No. The rest period allows recovery, but low blood counts and other problems can occur then too. Use the same urgent contact plan throughout the cycle.

questions.q: Can my morning and evening tablet numbers differ?
questions.a: Yes. The pharmacy may prescribe different morning and evening quantities to match the correct total daily dose. Do not assume the same number or substitute tablet strengths; follow the written label and calendar.

questions.q: Is the bevacizumab combination evidence the same?
questions.a: No. A study of Lonsurf plus bevacizumab tests an additional medicine and its extra risks. Its results should not be presented as the expected benefit of Lonsurf on its own.

chapters.title: Your tablet and rest-day plan
chapters.intro: A prescription calendar prevents dosing errors.

items.title: Take tablets after meals
items.text: Swallow the prescribed tablets with water within one hour after finishing breakfast and the evening meal on dosing days. Doses are based on body size and previous side effects; two tablet strengths may be combined. Some prescriptions have different morning and evening tablet quantities. Use the pharmacy calendar and do not calculate doses yourself.

items.title: Two blocks of five days
items.text: Take the prescribed morning and evening tablets on Days 1–5, have no Lonsurf on Days 6–7, then take morning and evening tablets on Days 8–12. Days 13–28 are tablet-free. A new 28-day cycle starts only when the team authorises it.

items.title: Missed, held or vomited doses

items.title: Baseline and each cycle
items.text: Blood count, kidney and liver tests and urine-protein screening are required. Additional blood counts may be needed during treatment, especially with kidney impairment.

items.title: Why a new cycle may wait
items.text: The blood-count requirements for starting another cycle are different from the thresholds for stopping tablets during a cycle. Symptoms, prior severe low counts, time to recover and the current prescription all matter.

items.title: Dose changes
items.text: Your team may delay treatment or use a lower dose after toxicity. Do not restart from a diary or increase the dose after a reduction. Tablet quantities are checked by pharmacy.

items.text: This oral medicine has moderate-to-high sickness risk. Agree a preventive and rescue anti-sickness plan with the team. If you cannot keep fluids or medicines down, call; do not add or repeat doses yourself.

items.title: Food, fluids and bowel symptoms
items.text: Take tablets after meals as instructed. Drink as your team advises and report diarrhoea, repeated vomiting, poor intake or reduced urine early. A prescribed bowel treatment plan does not replace urgent assessment.

items.title: Contraception and fertility
items.text: Discuss fertility before treatment. Women need highly effective contraception during treatment and for six months after; add a barrier method to hormonal contraception. Men with a partner who could become pregnant need effective contraception during treatment and for six months afterwards. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine.

items.title: Other medicines
items.text: Tell the pharmacist about all prescribed, non-prescription and herbal medicines, including antivirals. Keep tablets safely in their supplied packaging and follow disposal advice.

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

questions.q: Why do I need a check for varices?
questions.a: Liver disease can cause enlarged veins in the food pipe or stomach that may bleed. Bevacizumab can increase bleeding risk. The team checks for varices and treats any relevant risk before starting; having the test alone does not mean the risk has been controlled.

questions.q: Does an abnormal liver test always mean immune hepatitis?
questions.a: No. Liver cancer, underlying liver disease, infection, blocked bile flow and medicines can all affect results. The team compares results with your baseline and investigates the cause before deciding how each medicine changes.

questions.q: Can one medicine be held while the other continues?
questions.a: Sometimes. The reason for holding treatment, your general condition and the source rules for each medicine determine the plan. Never assume that stopping one means the other is automatically safe to continue.

questions.q: Do immune side effects stop when treatment stops?
questions.a: No. They can begin or persist afterwards. Keep the immunotherapy alert card and report new symptoms, including to doctors outside oncology.

questions.q: Does the thigh injection replace every drip?
questions.a: No. Atezolizumab may be given into the thigh, but bevacizumab remains an infusion into a vein. The two atezolizumab formulations have different doses and must be prescribed correctly.

clinical.component_rationale: Atezolizumab inhibits PD-L1-mediated immune suppression; bevacizumab inhibits VEGF signalling. The combination has distinct immune, vascular and underlying liver-disease safety domains.
key_points: NCCP 00831a: first systemic therapy for advanced/unresectable HCC; ECOG 0–1, Child-Pugh A.
Atezolizumab 1200 mg IV or 1875 mg SC then bevacizumab 15 mg/kg IV every 21 days; no dose reductions recommended.
Screen and manage oesophageal varices before treatment; recent bleeding/high-risk untreated varices require review.
HCC hepatitis thresholds depend on the matching baseline transaminase category; current LFTs alone do not establish immune causation.
NCCP Table 3 grading is CTCAE v4.0, not v5.0.
Bevacizumab 2+/3+ dipstick requires timed-protein follow-up; >2 to 4 g/24 h holds, >4 discontinues under NCCP. Nephrotic syndrome has an independent SmPC permanent-stop rule.
Persistent grade-3 hypertension, grade-4 VTE, grade≥3 bleeding, perforation and specified fistulae have distinct actions.
Counts are monitored without importing chemotherapy ANC/platelet dose thresholds.

patient_selection.treatment_intent: Disease control in previously untreated advanced/unresectable HCC.
disease_and_biomarker_context: NCCP 00831a: adults with advanced or unresectable HCC without previous systemic therapy; usual source eligibility includes ECOG 0–1 and Child-Pugh A liver function.
No PD-L1 testing requirement is specified for this HCC indication.
eligibility_orientation: Confirm Child-Pugh A, ECOG 0–1, no previous systemic HCC therapy and adequate organ function.
Assess varices, viral hepatitis, ascites, autoimmune disease, immunosuppression, bleeding/clotting and surgery risks.
important_cautions: No equivalent efficacy inference for Child-Pugh B/C or untreated high-risk varices.
Laboratory abnormalities require cause assessment; immune attribution is clinical.
The bevacizumab SmPC does not itself list HCC; HCC combination indication is supported by Tecentriq SmPC and NCCP.

support_summary: Screening and any required variceal treatment must be reviewed before starting. Call urgently for black stools or blood; vomiting blood or heavy bleeding needs emergency help.
Blood pressure and urine-protein checks are part of each cycle. Continue prescribed blood-pressure medicines and ask before changing them. A positive urine dipstick may need a timed urine collection.
Carry the supplied immunotherapy alert card during treatment and afterwards. New symptoms can need urgent treatment; do not wait for routine blood tests.

Both medicines have minimal sickness risk and routine preventive anti-sickness medicines or premedication are not usually required. The team individualises symptom treatment; do not self-treat new significant diarrhoea without advice.
Tell oncology before planned procedures and tell your dentist about bevacizumab. Wounds must heal and the team must agree an interruption/restart plan.

Discuss fertility and pregnancy prevention. Atezolizumab requires effective contraception for five months after the last dose and bevacizumab for six months; use the longer interval when both apply. Do not breastfeed during treatment or for at least six months after bevacizumab.

Warfarin: weekly INR until stable dose, then INR before each cycle.
Maintain immune alert and delayed-toxicity follow-up after stopping.
administration: IV atezolizumab is usually infused over 60 minutes initially and may take 30 minutes later if tolerated. The alternative 1875 mg thigh injection takes about seven minutes. Bevacizumab is still an IV infusion: usually 90 minutes first, then 60 and later 30 minutes if tolerated. Checks, preparation and observation make the whole visit longer.
Atezolizumab first, bevacizumab second. SC injection sites alternate thighs; avoid red/bruised/tender/hard skin. Maintain the planned three-week interval when rescheduling missed atezolizumab.
access: Anaphylaxis treatment facilities and suitable IV access are required even when atezolizumab is SC.
Rapid bevacizumab infusion is a separate off-label/local-policy option; it is not the default schedule here.

rationale.summary: This combination aims to control hepatocellular carcinoma, a cancer that starts in the liver, when it is advanced or cannot be removed and no previous systemic treatment has been given. Atezolizumab helps immune cells recognise cancer; bevacizumab blocks a signal that supports blood-vessel growth.
rationale.setting: First-line advanced or unresectable liver cancer (HCC)
factors: Liver function and variceal bleeding risk
Autoimmune/vascular disease, performance status and patient priorities
IV versus SC availability and separate component tolerability
alternatives: Discuss current MDT options, trials and supportive care including not proceeding; avoid cross-trial superiority claims.
limitations: The trial used IV atezolizumab and excluded important bleeding-risk groups. SC administration is supported by product and NCCP formulation evidence, not a separate HCC survival comparison. Other modern regimens require their own evidence discussion.
NCCP source reconciliation and software tests are not independent clinical approval.

evidence.population: 501 patients with previously untreated unresectable HCC, Child-Pugh A and ECOG 0–1, randomised 336 versus 165.
evidence.comparison: Atezolizumab 1200 mg IV plus bevacizumab 15 mg/kg every three weeks versus sorafenib.
evidence.applicability: The combination improved survival and time before cancer progressed in the study population. This does not predict an individual outcome or establish the same benefit for more severe liver dysfunction.

endpoints.metric: Median overall survival from randomisation; 31 August 2020 data cutoff
endpoints.interpretation: Updated ITT analysis; median follow-up 15.6 months. Group estimate for the selected first-line HCC population, not an individual prognosis.
endpoints.analysis_status: Updated published phase III analysis; descriptive p value

endpoints.metric: Median progression-free survival from randomisation; same 31 August 2020 cutoff
endpoints.interpretation: Updated whole-trial PFS; do not combine this endpoint with the earlier primary-analysis time point.
endpoints.analysis_status: Updated published phase III analysis

limitations: The trial used IV atezolizumab and excluded important bleeding-risk groups. SC administration is supported by product and NCCP formulation evidence, not a separate HCC survival comparison. Other modern regimens require their own evidence discussion.
Variceal bleeding within six months and untreated/incompletely treated varices with bleeding or high bleeding risk were excluded; safety cannot be assumed from screening alone.
Preserved liver function and trial selection limit extrapolation to decompensated cirrhosis.
evidence.harms: In the updated safety population, treatment-related grade 3–4 events occurred in 43% (143/329) with the combination and 46% (72/156) with sorafenib; treatment-related grade-5 events were 2% (6/329) and <1% (1/156). Types of harm differ; similar aggregate percentages do not make the treatments interchangeable.
